[2022]; Santomauro et al. [2021]; van Hoeken and Hoek [2020]). Further, over half of individuals with BED relapse or remain symptomatic following empirically supported BED treatments (Linardon [2018]; Sala et al. [2023]). Despite these adverse health impacts and suboptimal treatment outcomes, research on mechanisms that are theorized to contribute to BED maintenance and underlie individuals' engagement in disordered eating behaviors (DEBs) in their natural environments (e.g., at home, work/school) remains poorly understood. The limited research in this area serves as an important missed opportunity that, if addressed, may provide insight into mechanistic processes that may be leveraged for testing as treatment targets in novel real\\u2010time interventions and potentially improve BED outcomes.\\n\\n## Transdiagnostic Self\\u2010Regulatory Processes\\nSeveral BED theories posit that transdiagnostic self\\u2010regulatory processes\\u2014such as affect and emotion dysregulation\\u2014promote recurrent engagement in core disinhibited DEBs that characterize BED (e.g., loss of control [LOC] eating, binge eating) and contribute to BED maintenance (Hawkins and Clement [1984]; Heatherton and Baumeister [1991]; Mason et al. [2021]). Specifically, these theories posit that individuals attempt to distance themselves or \\u201cescape,\\u201d from adverse affective states that emerge on a moment\\u2010to\\u2010moment basis (e.g., high momentary negative affect, low momentary positive affect) by engaging in DEBs that can promote temporary affective improvements. In turn, these post\\u2010DEBs affective improvements can promote recurring DEBs and, over time, a negatively reinforced cycle that maintains BED (Hawkins and Clement [1984]; Heatherton and Baumeister [1991]; Mason et al. [2021]). Prior ecological momentary assessment (EMA) research has generally supported these hypotheses by demonstrating that individuals' negative affect levels progressively increase and positive affect levels decrease in the hours preceding LOC eating, overeating, and binge eating, and subsequently improve following the occurrence of these DEBs (Berg et al. [2017]; Schaefer et al. [2020]; Wonderlich et al. [2022]). Further, preliminary EMA research has also shown that greater momentary positive emotional eating (i.e., overeating in response to positive affect) significantly predicted greater momentary overeating among community\\u2010based and college women (Sultson et al. [2017]).\\n\\nComplementing this EMA research supporting these within\\u2010person (momentary, daily) processes, a large primarily between\\u2010person (cross\\u2010sectional) evidence\\u2010base that attests to trait\\u2010level processes indicates that it is not only dynamic moment\\u2010to\\u2010moment changes in the intensity or experience of affect (i.e., negatively and positively valenced emotional experiences) that promotes recurrent LOC eating and related disinhibited DEBs but emotion dysregulation (i.e., varied difficulties modulating emotions and behaviors) also upholds a vital role in this process (Lavender et al. [2015], [2014]; Prefit et al. [2019]). Although this research supports emotion dysregulation as a robust correlate of and mechanism that promotes BED pathology at the between\\u2010person level (Lavender et al. [2015], [2014]; Prefit et al. input.text: Characteristics for the present sample (N = 107) are reported in Table 1. Participants responded to 3131 out of 4494 possible surveys, reflecting good compliance (70.00%). Most participants identified as women (n = 88, 82.24%) and White (n = 99, 92.52%). On average, participants were 39.87 (SD = 13.35) years old and had a BMI of 35.10 (SD = 8.67). Further, participants generally reported LOC eating at a moderate level of severity across the assessed dimensions, yet with high variability (all ranges = 1-5): (1) general feeling of losing control while eating (M = 2.26, SD = 1.32); (2) difficulties resisting eating (M = 2.79, SD = 1.42); (3) difficulties stopping eating after starting (M = 2.54, SD = 1.41); (4) feeling driven or compelled to eat (M = 2.88, SD = 1.38); (5) not paying attention to one's eating (M = 3.45, SD = 1.18); (6) feeling disconnected while eating (M = 2.19, SD = 1.26). Further, a prior analysis of the present sample examined whether the momentary negative affect-binge eating association was mediated by negative urgency (i.e., a self-regulatory process that overlaps with emotion dysregulation [r = 0.948 in the present study] and is defined as behaving impulsively while experiencing negative affect). Regarding the direct effects, across models, there were significant positive associations between the negative affect and emotion dysregulation latent factors at the within-person (beta = 0.24) and between-person (beta = 0.90) levels, and inverse associations between the positive affect and emotion dysregulation factors at the within-person (beta = -0.08) - but not between-person - level. The emotion dysregulation factor mediated positive associations between the negative affect and feeling disconnected while eating factors at the within-person (beta = 0.03) and between-person (beta = 0.69) levels. There were also significant indirect effects at the within-person - but not between-person - level among the negative affect, emotion dysregulation, and (separately) general sense of LOC while eating, difficulties resisting eating, and feeling driven/compelled to eat factors (beta = 0.02-0.03). Adequate-to-good fit was defined as Comparative Fit Index and Tucker Lewis Index > 0.90, Root Mean Square Error of Approximation < 0.08, and Standardized Root Mean Square Residuals < 0.08.

In line with these recommended procedures, whether the data were missing at random (i.e., which is evident when missingness is dependent on observed values in a dataset) was assessed by creating missingness indicators that reflected whether (coded as 1) or not (coded as 0) data for the EMA-assessed constructs of interest in the present study were missing. These missingness indicators were then used as outcome variables in multilevel models (to account for the nested nature of the data structure) that examined whether missing EMA responses were meaningfully and influentially linked to various methodological factors, as well as demographic and psychological factors that were assessed at baseline. Meaningful/influential covariates were determined using Cohen\u2019s (1988) recommendations for small (R2 = 0.02), medium (R2 = 0.13), and large (R2 = 0.26) effects. Effects that were small to medium sized or larger (i.e., R2 \u2265 0.03), were considered influential. Effect sizes were used to identify influential correlates of missingness rather than p-values, as p-values are sample size dependent. Covariates that were identified as influential correlates of missingness (i.e., suggesting that the data were missing at random) were then included directly within the assessed statistical models. \n\nAs shown in full in Table S.7. below, effect sizes ranged from trivial to small in magnitude across the vast majority of models for all missingness tests. However, the data were generally shown to be missing at random relative to the survey number of the day (1-6; R2s = 0.029), but not other methodological (e.g., compliance, day in the study, treatment group), baseline demographic (e.g., gender, BMI), or baseline psychopathological factors (e.g., trait-level ED pathology, trait-level emotion dysregulation). To adjust for this, survey number of the day was controlled in all models (Enders, 2022). \n\nData were not suggested to be missing not at random (i.e., when missingness is dependent on psychological factors that are linked to the targeted population, which in this case would be suggested by eating disorder-related psychopathology). This was determined via the trivial associations that were identified for associations between baseline Eating Disorder Examination Global Scores (R2s = 0) and Clinical Impairment Assessment for Eating Disorders Total Scores (R2s = 0). hypotheses.statement: Momentary emotion dysregulation mediates momentary associations between negative affect and loss-of-control (LOC) eating.

findings.location: Results, paragraph 1
findings.quote: Participants responded to 3131 out of 4494 possible surveys, reflecting good compliance (70.00%).
findings.notes: 3131/4494 = 69.67%, not the printed 70.00%; the printed figure implies a denominator of about 4473. The denominator itself is internally coherent: 107 participants x 6 surveys per day x 7 days = 4494, so it is built on the analytic sample rather than the 112 enrolled (which would give 4704). The most likely innocent explanation is that 70.00% is the MEAN of participants' individual compliance rates rather than the pooled ratio printed beside it; the two quantities differ whenever compliance varies across participants, and the paper does not say which it reports. A second possibility is simple rounding-up of 69.67% to a presentational 70%. Either way the sentence pairs a count, a denominator and a percentage that do not reconcile, and the exactly-round 70.00% to two decimals is what makes it worth a query rather than a shrug.

consequence.explanation: Affects only the descriptive characterisation of EMA compliance as 'good'; no inferential result in Table 2 depends on this figure.

findings.location: Table 2, 'Direct effects' block, third row of all six models
findings.quote: Positive affect ➔ Emotion dysregulation ➔ LOC eating	0.28 (0.07)	< 0.001	0.13	0.82 (0.41)	0.048	0.68

reported.printed_row_label: Positive affect ➔ Emotion dysregulation ➔ LOC eating

computed.identification: This row occupies the b-path slot of a 1-1-1 mediation model. A complete mediation model has exactly five direct paths (a1: NA->ED, a2: PA->ED, b: ED->LOC, c1': NA->LOC, c2': PA->LOC) and the Direct effects block prints exactly five rows, of which the other four are correctly labelled; the remaining slot must therefore be ED->LOC.
computed.corroboration_1: The body text attributes these exact values to the emotion-dysregulation-to-LOC direct effect: within-person beta 0.13-0.14 and between-person beta 0.68-0.77 correspond to Model 1 (0.13/0.68) and Model 6 (0.14/0.77) in this row.
computed.corroboration_2: The parallel supplementary table (Data S1, Table S.4) labels the analogous row 'Emotion Dysregulation à LOC Eating'.
computed.corroboration_3: The identical label already appears in the Indirect effects block of the same model, carrying different values (0.28 vs -0.02 in Model 1).

findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a cross-reference contradiction between a printed row label, the structure of the model, and the body text, not an arithmetic result.
findings.notes: A two-step mediational path cannot by definition appear under 'Direct effects', and the same label appearing twice within one model block with different numbers makes the duplication self-evident. The values themselves are not in question -- the regression check reconciles every one of them -- so this is a labelling defect, not a data defect. It nonetheless mislabels the b-path, which is the single load-bearing coefficient of the paper's mediation argument, and it does so identically in all six models, so a reader working from Table 2 alone would misread the paper's central result. Most plausibly a copy-paste of the Indirect-effects row label during table preparation.

consequence.explanation: The emotion-dysregulation-to-LOC-eating direct effect, which the Results section discusses at length as beta = 0.13-0.14 (within) and 0.68-0.77 (between), is printed under a label describing a different path in all six models.

findings.location: Table 2, all 84 coefficients (6 models x 7 paths x 2 levels)
findings.quote: Note: Bold text is used to reflect significant effects, defined as p < 0.05; momentary observations at level 1 were nested within participants at level 2

reported.format: b (SE) with a separate p column

findings.notes: Every one of the 84 printed (b, SE, p) triples reconciles under the Wald test t = b/SE at any degrees of freedom from 30 upward, which covers every value plausible for this design (107 participants at level 2, 3131 observations at level 1). The tool nevertheless returns `indeterminate` rather than `consistent`, and correctly so: the paper prints no df, the verdict would change at df = 10, and that df is this review's assumption rather than the authors' number. Recorded as a refusal so it is not read as a clean bill the paper did not earn. Two caveats on the method: indirect-effect p-values in MSEM may come from a delta-method or bootstrap procedure rather than a Wald test, in which case exact agreement is not required; and at 2 printed decimals many of these rounding intervals are wide enough that the check has little power (see table2_coefficient_precision).

consequence.explanation: No reported coefficient contradicts its own standard error and p-value; the refusal concerns a missing df, not a discrepancy.

findings.notes: This is a finding about REPORTING PRECISION, not about the authors' arithmetic. Table 2 prints b and SE to two decimals for coefficients whose magnitude is 0.01-0.02, so the printed values carry almost no information about the test: a 95% interval built from them excludes zero while the paper reports p = 0.065. The paper's own p-value is the authoritative number here and there is no reason to doubt it -- the discrepancy is entirely an artifact of rounding a value of 0.0x to two places. The consequence is that a reader cannot independently verify any of the small indirect effects from Table 2 as printed. inputs.family_label: Within-person indirect (mediation) effects: negative and positive affect -> emotion dysregulation -> each of 6 LOC eating dimensions, all on the same 107 participants (Table 2)

findings.reproduction: metascience multiplicity --family-label "Within-person indirect effects, 2 predictors x 6 LOC dimensions, Table 2" --tests '[{"p_value":0.001},{"p_value":0.026},{"p_value":0.154},{"p_value":0.001},{"p_value":0.858},{"p_value":0.001},{"p_value":0.07},{"p_value":0.122},{"p_value":0.233},{"p_value":0.067},{"p_value":0.859},{"p_value":0.065}]' --alpha 0.05
findings.notes: The family chosen is the paper's own primary claim set: the same 107 participants, one stated aim, two predictors crossed with six LOC eating outcomes. That choice is a judgement and the tool cannot make it. Uncorrected testing at this scale is entirely ordinary in this literature and this is not an accusation; the arithmetic simply says what the numbers imply. Three of the four significant within-person indirect effects (the three at p = 0.001) survive every correction including Benjamini-Yekutieli, which is the appropriate one here because the six LOC dimensions are strongly correlated (Data S1 Table S.2 reports momentary covariances of 0.66-0.73 among four of them). The one claim that does not survive is the difficulties-resisting-eating pathway at p = 0.026, and it is named in the abstract and conclusions alongside the three robust ones. Note also that the exploratory analyses add a further 24 tests of the reversed pathway, so 12 is a floor on the true comparison count.

consequence.explanation: The within-person indirect effect on difficulties resisting eating (p = 0.026) does not survive any of the four corrections, yet is presented in the conclusions on equal footing with the three pathways that do.

findings.location: Results, Indirect Effects paragraph; Table 2, Model 3 within-person indirect effect
findings.quote: The emotion dysregulation factors did not mediate associations between the negative affect factors and either the difficulties stopping eating after starting or the not paying attention to one's eating factors
findings.notes: The paper builds a substantive interpretation on this null -- it argues in the Discussion that 'there was greater variability in whether moment-to-moment changes in the two self-regulatory factors promoted this LOC eating outcome' and offers explanations (others entering the room, alternative coping behaviours) for why the pathway is absent. But the data are compatible with an indirect effect up to 0.099, which is LARGER than the three indirect effects the paper reports as significant (0.10, 0.09, 0.09 in Models 1, 4 and 6). The distinction being drawn between dimensions that do and do not show mediation is therefore not established by these intervals. No smallest effect size of interest is stated anywhere in the paper, so equivalence cannot be tested and no conclusion of 'no effect' is licensed. The interval here is derived by this review from the printed b and SE, not printed by the authors -- the paper reports no confidence intervals for any coefficient in Table 2.

consequence.explanation: The paper's headline claim that mediation 'varied across LOC eating dimensions' rests on contrasting significant with non-significant pathways whose intervals overlap substantially.

computed.identification_status: df = 0 means the model is just-identified (saturated): it has as many free parameters as observed moments and therefore reproduces the data exactly by construction

findings.notes: The paper states 'The factor structure of these constructs was confirmed in the present sample via multilevel confirmatory factor analyses' and, for emotion dysregulation specifically, 'The factor structure was confirmed via MCFA in the present sample following minor modifications'. For the emotion dysregulation factor that confirmation cannot have come from these fit statistics: at df = 0 the model is saturated and perfect fit is guaranteed regardless of the data. This matters more than a typical fit-index quibble because emotion dysregulation is the mediator in all six primary models, and because the Methods say this was the one measurement model that required modification -- modifications were accepted on the basis of AIC and sample-size-adjusted BIC decreasing, which is a defensible criterion, but the fit indices printed beside them are not evidence. An innocent reading is that the authors report the row for completeness rather than as evidence; the paper does not distinguish it from the two informative rows above it.

consequence.explanation: The claim that the emotion dysregulation factor structure was 'confirmed' by MCFA is not supported by the fit statistics reported for it, because a just-identified model cannot fail them.

findings.location: Data S1, Table S.6, Baseline Beck Depression Inventory row; Methods, Participants and Procedures
findings.quote: Baseline Beck Depression Inventory Total Score	1.257	.212	0.736	-0.418, 1.886
findings.notes: The paper states flatly that 'Participants without sufficient data did not differ from those in the analytic sample on baseline methodological, demographic, or psychopathological factors.' With only 5 excluded participants, that conclusion is not supportable from these data: the BDI interval is compatible with the excluded participants being up to 1.886 standard deviations more depressed, an enormous effect, and the point estimate d = 0.736 is itself a large effect that is non-significant only because n = 5. Three further rows show medium-to-large point estimates in the same situation (age d = -0.591, BMI d = -0.563, DERS d = 0.453). No smallest effect size of interest is stated, so equivalence cannot be tested. A second, independent problem with the same table: the chi-squared tests on gender and treatment completion status have expected cell counts far below 5 in the excluded group, which violates the chi-squared approximation. None of this suggests anything improper -- 5 exclusions out of 112 is a good retention rate and the authors were right to check -- but the check cannot bear the weight the Methods sentence puts on it, and the honest statement is that comparability could not be established rather than that it was.

consequence.explanation: The Methods assertion that excluded and included participants did not differ is not established by these intervals, which remain compatible with large baseline differences in depression, age and BMI.

findings.location: Data S1, Table S.6, Baseline Beck Depression Inventory row
findings.quote: Baseline Beck Depression Inventory Total Score	1.257	.212	0.736	-0.418, 1.886
findings.notes: The tool returned `suspicious` on the ground that the p recovered from the interval (0.2105) differs from the printed p (0.212). I record this a rung lower, at `indeterminate`, because the two numbers are produced by different procedures and are not required to agree: the printed p comes from the independent-samples t-test (t = 1.257, df = 110), whereas the 95% interval is an interval for Cohen's d, conventionally built from the noncentral t distribution, which is not symmetric and does not invert to the t-test p. The estimate sits essentially at its interval's midpoint (0.734 against a printed 0.736), so the interval and the point estimate are mutually coherent. The residual discrepancy is 0.0015 and carries no interpretive consequence. Flagging this as a defect would be a false accusation against a standard reporting convention.

consequence.explanation: A 0.0015 difference between two p-values computed by different standard procedures; nothing in the paper depends on it.

computed.internal_tension_in_the_same_sentence: 'small' is defined as R2 = 0.02 but 'small to medium sized or larger' is then glossed as R2 >= 0.03, so the rule does not follow from the benchmark it cites

findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a contradiction between a stated decision rule and its application, established by comparing two printed numbers.
findings.notes: Survey number of the day is the sole covariate included in all twelve models (six primary, six exploratory), and its inclusion is justified by the missing-data analysis. But its R-squared of 0.029 does not meet the R2 >= 0.03 rule the same note states, and the rule itself does not follow from the Cohen benchmark it cites in the preceding sentence (small is given as 0.02). Two innocent readings are available and either may be right: the authors may have applied a >= 0.02 rule consistent with the cited benchmark and mis-transcribed it as 0.03, or 0.029 may be a rounded display of a value at or above 0.030. Both would be transcription rather than analytic errors. It is worth a query because the sentence is load-bearing -- it is the entire justification for the model's only covariate -- and because as printed the rule excludes the variable it was used to include. Note also that 0.02/0.13/0.26 are Cohen's benchmarks for f-squared rather than R-squared, though the paper's usage is common in practice.

consequence.explanation: The stated covariate-selection rule, as printed, excludes the survey-number covariate that was in fact included in all twelve models.

findings.notes: Recorded deliberately as a NON-finding. An 84-cell table in which six supposedly separate columns are identical to three decimals is exactly the pattern a duplication check would escalate on, and it has an airtight innocent explanation stated in the paper's own Methods: 'Participants were presented with the LOC eating items if they endorsed that they ate since their last survey.' All six items are therefore missing or present together, the six missingness indicators are one and the same variable, and five of the six columns are redundant rather than duplicated. detect_duplication was not run on this table because its unit is (mean, SD) pairs and these are single R-squared values; the guard here is the design, not a statistic.

First, several of the checks in this review returned `indeterminate` only because the degrees of freedom and the unrounded coefficients were not printed -- both would be immediately resolvable from the model output. findings.location: Results, paragraph 1
findings.quote: Participants responded to 3131 out of 4494 possible surveys, reflecting good compliance (70.00%).

computed.tool_actually_used: check_count_percent (MCP), which the findings-schema technique enum has no entry for

findings.notes: Produced by the check_count_percent tool, not by hand; recorded under no_tool_exists only because the schema's technique enum has no entry for that tool. 3131/4494 = 69.67%, not the printed 70.00%; the printed figure implies a denominator of about 4473. The denominator itself is internally coherent: 107 participants x 6 surveys per day x 7 days = 4494, so it is built on the analytic sample rather than the 112 enrolled (which would give 4704). The most likely innocent explanation is that 70.00% is the MEAN of participants' individual compliance rates rather than the pooled ratio printed beside it; the two differ whenever compliance varies across participants, and the paper does not say which it reports. A second possibility is presentational rounding of 69.67%. Either way the sentence pairs a count, a denominator and a percentage that do not reconcile, and the exactly-round 70.00% to two decimals is what makes it worth a query rather than a shrug.

consequence.explanation: Affects only the descriptive characterisation of EMA compliance as 'good'; no inferential result in Table 2 depends on this figure.

findings.location: Table 2, 'Direct effects' block, third row of all six models
findings.quote: Positive affect ➔ Emotion dysregulation ➔ LOC eating	0.28 (0.07)	< 0.001	0.13	0.82 (0.41)	0.048	0.68

reported.printed_row_label: Positive affect ➔ Emotion dysregulation ➔ LOC eating

computed.identification: This row occupies the b-path slot of a 1-1-1 mediation model. A complete mediation model has exactly five direct paths (a1: NA->ED, a2: PA->ED, b: ED->LOC, c1': NA->LOC, c2': PA->LOC) and the Direct effects block prints exactly five rows, of which the other four are correctly labelled; the remaining slot must therefore be ED->LOC.
computed.corroboration_1: The body text attributes these exact values to the emotion-dysregulation-to-LOC direct effect: within-person beta 0.13-0.14 and between-person beta 0.68-0.77 correspond to Model 1 (0.13/0.68) and Model 6 (0.14/0.77) in this row.
computed.corroboration_2: The parallel supplementary table (Data S1, Table S.4) labels the analogous row 'Emotion Dysregulation to LOC Eating'.
computed.corroboration_3: The identical label already appears in the Indirect effects block of the same model, carrying different values (0.28 vs -0.02 in Model 1).

findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a cross-reference contradiction between a printed row label, the structure of the model, and the body text, not an arithmetic result.
findings.notes: A two-step mediational path cannot by definition appear under 'Direct effects', and the same label appearing twice within one model block with different numbers makes the duplication self-evident. The values themselves are not in question -- the regression check reconciles every one of them -- so this is a labelling defect, not a data defect. It nonetheless mislabels the b-path, which is the single load-bearing coefficient of the paper's mediation argument, and does so identically in all six models, so a reader working from Table 2 alone would misread the paper's central result. Most plausibly a copy-paste of the Indirect-effects row label during table preparation.

consequence.explanation: The emotion-dysregulation-to-LOC-eating direct effect, which the Results section discusses at length as beta = 0.13-0.14 (within) and 0.68-0.77 (between), is printed under a label describing a different path in all six models.

findings.location: Table 2, all 84 coefficients (6 models x 7 paths x 2 levels)
findings.quote: Note: Bold text is used to reflect significant effects, defined as p < 0.05; momentary observations at level 1 were nested within participants at level 2

reported.format: b (SE) with a separate p column

findings.notes: Every one of the 84 printed (b, SE, p) triples reconciles under the Wald test t = b/SE at any degrees of freedom from 30 upward, which covers every value plausible for this design (107 participants at level 2, 3131 observations at level 1). The tool nevertheless returns `indeterminate` rather than `consistent`, and correctly so: the paper prints no df, the verdict would change at df = 10, and that df is this review's assumption rather than the authors' number. Recorded as a refusal so it is not read as a clean bill the paper did not earn. Two caveats on method: indirect-effect p-values in MSEM may come from a delta-method or bootstrap procedure rather than a Wald test, in which case exact agreement is not required; and at 2 printed decimals many of these rounding intervals are wide enough that the check has little power (see table2_coefficient_precision).

consequence.explanation: No reported coefficient contradicts its own standard error and p-value; the refusal concerns a missing df, not a discrepancy.

findings.location: Table 2, Indirect effects rows (e.g. Model 6, positive affect within-person)
findings.quote: Also, all momentary mediational pathways involving positive affect as a predictor were not significant.

computed.implied_t_range_across_printed_rounding: b in [0.015,0.025] over se in [0.005,0.015] gives absolute t anywhere from 1.0 to 5.0

findings.notes: This is a finding about REPORTING PRECISION, not about the authors' arithmetic. Table 2 prints b and SE to two decimals for coefficients whose magnitude is 0.01-0.02, so the printed values carry almost no information about the test: a 95% interval built from them excludes zero while the paper reports p = 0.065. The paper's own p-value is the authoritative number here and there is no reason to doubt it -- the discrepancy is entirely an artifact of rounding a value of 0.0x to two places. The consequence is that a reader cannot independently verify any of the small indirect effects from Table 2 as printed. The supplement's Table S.4 prints the same class of quantity to three decimals, which is sufficient; the main table does not.

consequence.explanation: None of the twelve within-person indirect effects in Table 2 can be checked against their own printed b and SE, because two-decimal rounding of coefficients near 0.01 leaves the implied test statistic unconstrained.

findings.location: Table 2, Indirect effects rows, within-person columns (12 tests)
findings.quote: Note: Bold text is used to reflect significant effects, defined as p < 0.05

inputs.family_label: Within-person indirect (mediation) effects: negative and positive affect -> emotion dysregulation -> each of 6 LOC eating dimensions, all on the same 107 participants (Table 2)

findings.reproduction: metascience multiplicity --family-label "Within-person indirect effects, 2 predictors x 6 LOC dimensions, Table 2" --tests '[{"p_value":0.001},{"p_value":0.026},{"p_value":0.154},{"p_value":0.001},{"p_value":0.858},{"p_value":0.001},{"p_value":0.07},{"p_value":0.122},{"p_value":0.233},{"p_value":0.067},{"p_value":0.859},{"p_value":0.065}]' --alpha 0.05
findings.notes: The family chosen is the paper's own primary claim set: the same 107 participants, one stated aim, two predictors crossed with six LOC eating outcomes. That choice is a judgement and the tool cannot make it. Uncorrected testing at this scale is entirely ordinary in this literature and this is not an accusation; the arithmetic simply says what the numbers imply. Three of the four significant within-person indirect effects (the three at p = 0.001) survive every correction including Benjamini-Yekutieli, which is the appropriate one here because the six LOC dimensions are strongly correlated (Data S1 Table S.2 reports momentary covariances of 0.66-0.73 among four of them). The one claim that does not survive is the difficulties-resisting-eating pathway at p = 0.026, and it is named in the abstract and conclusions alongside the three robust ones. Note also that the exploratory analyses add a further 24 tests of the reversed pathway, so 12 is a floor on the true comparison count.

consequence.explanation: The within-person indirect effect on difficulties resisting eating (p = 0.026) does not survive any of the four corrections, yet is presented in the conclusions on equal footing with the three pathways that do.

findings.location: Results, Indirect Effects paragraph; Table 2, Model 3 within-person indirect effect
findings.quote: The emotion dysregulation factors did not mediate associations between the negative affect factors and either the difficulties stopping eating after starting or the not paying attention to one's eating factors
findings.notes: The paper builds a substantive interpretation on this null -- it argues in the Discussion that 'there was greater variability in whether moment-to-moment changes in the two self-regulatory factors promoted this LOC eating outcome' and offers explanations (others entering the room, alternative coping behaviours) for why the pathway is absent. But the data are compatible with an indirect effect up to 0.099, which is LARGER than the three indirect effects the paper reports as significant (0.10, 0.09, 0.09 in Models 1, 4 and 6). The distinction being drawn between dimensions that do and do not show mediation is therefore not established by these intervals. No smallest effect size of interest is stated anywhere in the paper, so equivalence cannot be tested and no conclusion of 'no effect' is licensed. The interval here is derived by this review from the printed b and SE, not printed by the authors -- the paper reports no confidence intervals for any coefficient in Table 2.

consequence.explanation: The paper's headline claim that mediation 'varied across LOC eating dimensions' rests on contrasting significant with non-significant pathways whose intervals overlap substantially.

The 3 not_run cells are the BDI, CIA and DERS totals: these are multi-item composites whose scoring convention -- sum or mean of items -- the paper never states, and running GRIM/GRIMMER at the wrong granularity is precisely how false impossibilities are manufactured. findings.notes: Every one of the 24 exploratory coefficients reconciles with its own standard error and p-value at any df of 30 or more. Because the supplement prints to three decimals rather than two, these checks have real power -- several rows reconcile strictly rather than only through the printed-precision grace path, which is stronger evidence. As with Table 2 the aggregate is clamped to `indeterminate` solely because the paper prints no df. Also verified as a cross-reference: the four exploratory pathways the Results text names as significant (general LOC eating, difficulties resisting eating, driven/compelled to eat, felt disconnected) are exactly the four with within-person p < .05 in Table S.4 (.008, .043, .013, .049), and the two named as non-significant are exactly the two that are not (.611, .054).

findings.location: Data S1, Table S.4, Model 6, within-person indirect effect of emotion dysregulation via negative affect
findings.quote: Emotion Dysregulation à Negative Affect à LOC Eating	0.076 (0.039)	.049	0.039
findings.notes: No discrepancy is alleged: the reported p = .049 lies inside the interval [.047, .056] that the printed b and SE permit, so the check passes. It is recorded because the point estimate 0.076/0.039 implies p = .051, and this row is one of the four the paper counts as a significant exploratory pathway. Whether it falls on the significant side of .05 cannot be determined from the values as printed -- that depends on digits the supplement does not show. This is a fragility in one secondary claim, not evidence of error, and the innocent reading (the authors hold the unrounded values and .049 is correct) is the likely one.

consequence.explanation: One of the four exploratory pathways the paper reports as significant sits at the alpha boundary and cannot be independently confirmed as significant from the printed values.

findings.quote: Emotion Dysregulation	0.034 (0)	1.000	1.000	1.000	0.000

computed.identification_status: df = 0 means the model is just-identified (saturated): it has as many free parameters as observed moments and therefore reproduces the data exactly by construction
computed.consequence_for_fit_indices: CFI = 1.000, TLI = 1.000 and RMSEA = 0.000 are the values a saturated model must return and carry no information about whether the factor structure is correct

findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a reading of the reported degrees of freedom, not a recomputation. recalc_stat_to_p cannot convert a chi-squared at df = 0, which is itself the point.
findings.notes: The paper states 'The factor structure of these constructs was confirmed in the present sample via multilevel confirmatory factor analyses' and, for emotion dysregulation specifically, 'The factor structure was confirmed via MCFA in the present sample following minor modifications'. For the emotion dysregulation factor that confirmation cannot have come from these fit statistics: at df = 0 the model is saturated and perfect fit is guaranteed regardless of the data. This matters more than a typical fit-index quibble because emotion dysregulation is the mediator in all six primary models, and because the Methods say this was the one measurement model that required modification -- modifications were accepted on the basis of AIC and sample-size-adjusted BIC decreasing, which is a defensible criterion, but the fit indices printed beside them are not evidence. An innocent reading is that the authors report the row for completeness rather than as evidence; the paper does not distinguish it from the two informative rows above it.

consequence.explanation: The claim that the emotion dysregulation factor structure was 'confirmed' by MCFA is not supported by the fit statistics reported for it, because a just-identified model cannot fail them.

findings.notes: Both representative attrition tests reproduce their reported p-values essentially exactly. The df were not printed by the paper and were inferred from the design (110 = 107 + 5 - 2 for the t-tests; 2 for the completion-status chi-squared, recovered as the value that reproduces the printed p). findings.location: Data S1, Table S.6, Baseline Beck Depression Inventory row; Methods, Participants and Procedures
findings.quote: Baseline Beck Depression Inventory Total Score	1.257	.212	0.736	-0.418, 1.886
findings.notes: The paper states flatly that 'Participants without sufficient data did not differ from those in the analytic sample on baseline methodological, demographic, or psychopathological factors.' With only 5 excluded participants that conclusion is not supportable from these data: the BDI interval is compatible with the excluded participants being up to 1.886 standard deviations more depressed, and the point estimate d = 0.736 is itself a large effect that is non-significant only because n = 5. Three further rows show medium-to-large point estimates in the same situation (age d = -0.591, BMI d = -0.563, DERS d = 0.453). No smallest effect size of interest is stated, so equivalence cannot be tested. A second, independent problem with the same table: the chi-squared tests on gender and treatment completion status have expected cell counts far below 5 in the excluded group, which violates the chi-squared approximation (rulebook rule 5). None of this suggests anything improper -- 5 exclusions out of 112 is a good retention rate and the authors were right to check -- but the check cannot bear the weight the Methods sentence puts on it, and the honest statement is that comparability could not be established rather than that it was.

consequence.explanation: The Methods assertion that excluded and included participants did not differ is not established by these intervals, which remain compatible with large baseline differences in depression, age and BMI.

findings.location: Data S1, Table S.6, Baseline Beck Depression Inventory row
findings.quote: Baseline Beck Depression Inventory Total Score	1.257	.212	0.736	-0.418, 1.886
findings.notes: The tool returned `suspicious` on the ground that the p recovered from the interval (0.2105) differs from the printed p (0.212). I record this a rung lower, at `indeterminate`, because the two numbers are produced by different procedures and are not required to agree: the printed p comes from the independent-samples t-test (t = 1.257, df = 110), whereas the 95% interval is an interval for Cohen's d, conventionally built from the noncentral t distribution, which is not symmetric and does not invert to the t-test p. The estimate sits essentially at its interval's midpoint (0.734 against a printed 0.736), so interval and point estimate are mutually coherent. The residual discrepancy is 0.0015 and carries no interpretive consequence. Flagging it as a defect would be a false accusation against a standard reporting convention.

consequence.explanation: A 0.0015 difference between two p-values computed by different standard procedures; nothing in the paper depends on it.

findings.location: Data S1, Table S.7 note and Missing Data Analyses text; Methods, Statistical Analyses
findings.quote: Meaningful/influential covariates were determined using Cohen’s (1988) recommendations for small (R2 = 0.02), medium (R2 = 0.13), and large (R2 = 0.26) effects. Effects that were small to medium sized or larger (i.e., R2 ≥ 0.03), were considered influential.

computed.comparison: 0.029 < 0.030, so the only covariate carried into the models falls below the paper's own stated inclusion threshold
computed.internal_tension_in_the_same_sentence: 'small' is defined as R2 = 0.02 but 'small to medium sized or larger' is then glossed as R2 >= 0.03, so the rule does not follow from the benchmark it cites

findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a contradiction between a stated decision rule and its application, established by comparing two printed numbers.
findings.notes: Survey number of the day is the sole covariate included in all twelve models (six primary, six exploratory), and its inclusion is justified by the missing-data analysis. But its R-squared of 0.029 does not meet the R2 >= 0.03 rule the same note states, and the rule itself does not follow from the Cohen benchmark cited in the preceding sentence (small is given as 0.02). Two innocent readings are available and either may be right: the authors may have applied a >= 0.02 rule consistent with the cited benchmark and mis-transcribed it as 0.03, or 0.029 may be a rounded display of a value at or above 0.030. Both would be transcription rather than analytic errors. It is worth a query because the sentence is load-bearing -- it is the entire justification for the model's only covariate -- and because as printed the rule excludes the variable it was used to include. Note also that 0.02/0.13/0.26 are Cohen's benchmarks for f-squared rather than R-squared, though the paper's usage is common in practice.

consequence.explanation: The stated covariate-selection rule, as printed, excludes the survey-number covariate that was in fact included in all twelve models.

findings.location: Data S1, Table S.7, all six missingness-indicator columns

reported.pattern: every covariate's R-squared is identical to three decimals across all six missingness indicators

computed.design_explanation: The six LOC eating items were administered as a block, conditional on the participant reporting having eaten, so the missingness indicator is the SAME binary variable for all six items; identical predictors regressed on an identical outcome must return identical R-squared.

findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a design-based explanation of an observed repetition, recorded to prevent it being mistaken for duplication.
findings.notes: Recorded deliberately as a NON-finding. An 84-cell table in which six supposedly separate columns are identical to three decimals is exactly the pattern a duplication check would escalate on, and it has an airtight innocent explanation stated in the paper's own Methods: 'Participants were presented with the LOC eating items if they endorsed that they ate since their last survey.' All six items are therefore missing or present together, the six missingness indicators are one and the same variable, and five of the six columns are redundant rather than duplicated. detect_duplication was not run on this table because its unit is (mean, SD) pairs and these are single R-squared values; the guard here is the design, not a statistic.

Low consequence for the results, but it is the second labelling defect of the same kind in this paper -- the first being the mislabelled b-path row in Table 2 -- and together they suggest the tables were assembled by copying and editing rows without a final consistency pass.

This is almost certainly a dropped digit rather than anything substantive -- the parent trial plainly exists and is cited to Peterson et al. (2020) -- but it appears in the one sentence a reader would use to locate the protocol, and the protocol is what would establish whether any of this paper's hypotheses were specified in advance. This is an extremely common statement in this literature and carries no suggestion of impropriety, but it is worth recording for two specific reasons here. First, several checks in this review returned `indeterminate` only because the degrees of freedom and the unrounded coefficients were not printed -- both would be immediately resolvable from the model output. Second, the paper reports sensitivity analyses ('Sensitivity analyses showed that the overall pattern of results was consistent when data from assessments that followed eating episodes only were used') whose results appear nowhere in the article or the supplement, so a reader cannot check that claim at all.

findings.notes: The level-1 sample size for the paper's six primary models is never given. This is the missing quantity behind several refusals in this review: without it, and without the model degrees of freedom, the reported standard errors cannot be independently anchored. It also bears on interpretation, since the between-person estimates rest on 107 participants but the within-person estimates rest on an unstated and possibly much smaller number of eating-episode observations. Recorded as indeterminate rather than as a defect: reporting level-1 N is good practice and its absence is common, but here it is the specific thing that prevents verification.

consequence.explanation: The observation count underlying every within-person estimate in Table 2 is not reported, so those estimates cannot be independently anchored.
